summary: DHCP FORCERENEW lets a server force a client to renew its lease. In this protocol the server sends a nonce in the initial DHCP ACK, and the client uses it later to validate FORCERENEW messages. It updates RFC 3203.

plainLanguage.summary: The server gives you a secret word. Later, a message to renew your address only counts if it has that word.

questions: what is dhcp forcerenew nonce authentication
subtitle: A way to authenticate DHCPv4 FORCERENEW messages with a per-client nonce, without distributing keys out of band.

tldr.problem: DHCP FORCERENEW must be authenticated with RFC 3118, which needs a constant token or shared secret to be distributed to clients out of band. That is more than this use case needs and has limited adoption of FORCERENEW.
tldr.mechanism: The server sends a 128-bit nonce to the client in the initial DHCP ACK. Later FORCERENEW messages carry an HMAC-MD5 digest computed with that nonce, which the client checks.
tldr.outcome: Off-network attackers cannot make a client renew at a time of their choosing, because they do not have the nonce. The RFC updates RFC 3203.

today: RFC 6704 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2012 that updates RFC 3203. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why FORCERENEW Needs Lighter Authentication
sections.content:
The DHCP reconfigure extension in RFC 3203 lets a server trigger reconfiguration of a single host. It requires every Forcerenew message to be authenticated using RFC 3118, which in turn needs a constant token or shared secret to be distributed to clients out of band.

The reason for mandatory authentication is to stop an off-network attacker from predicting when a renewal will happen. Without FORCERENEW, renewal timing is under the client's control and the attacker cannot see the exchange.

The RFC argues that the RFC 3118 requirement is more stringent than this use case needs and has limited adoption of FORCERENEW. RFC 6704 borrows the nonce idea from DHCPv6 (RFC 3315) and defines a new authentication protocol for DHCPv4 FORCERENEW that needs no out-of-band key distribution. It updates RFC 3203.
sections.plainLanguage: The old rule was like needing a secret handshake taught to everyone in advance. This one lets the server hand out the secret on the spot.

sections.title: How the Nonce Protocol Works
sections.content:
A Forcerenew message MUST now be authenticated using either RFC 3118 or the Forcerenew Nonce Authentication protocol. The new protocol protects a client against misconfiguration caused by a Forcerenew message from a malicious DHCP server.

The server sends a Forcerenew Nonce to the client in the initial exchange of DHCP messages. The client records it. The server then includes a Hashed Message Authentication Code (HMAC) computed from the nonce in later Forcerenew messages. Both the nonce and the HMAC are carried as authentication information in a DHCP Authentication option.

The protocol is used only if the client and server are not using the RFC 3118 mechanism and have negotiated to use it.
sections.plainLanguage: The server gives you a secret word once. After that, every 'please check in' note has a stamp that only someone who knows the word can make.

sections.title: Negotiating Support
sections.content:
A client signals support by including a FORCERENEW_NONCE_CAPABLE option (code 145) in its DHCP Discover and Request messages. The option holds the code, a length n and a list of algorithms the client supports. This document defines algorithm 1 with type 2; other values are left to future documents.

A server that does not support the protocol SHOULD ignore the option. A server that does support it and requires it puts the same option in its DHCPOFFER. The server SHOULD NOT include the option unless the client indicated capability, and a client may prefer capable servers when several offers arrive. A capable server MUST include the option in all offers, and a client that supports the mechanism MUST include it in all Discover and Request messages.

If the client's message lacks the option, the server MUST NOT include a Forcerenew Nonce authentication option in the DHCP ACK. A client MUST NOT send DHCP messages with authentication options whose protocol value is Forcerenew Nonce Authentication.
sections.plainLanguage: Before using the secret word, both sides say 'I know this trick'. If one side does not, they skip it.

sections.title: The Authentication Option Format
sections.content:
The protocol reuses the DHCP authentication option format from RFC 3118 and the Reconfigure Key Authentication Protocol from RFC 3315. The option fields are set as follows: Code 90 (Authentication), Length (the length of the protocol), Protocol 3 (Reconfigure Key), Algorithm 1 (HMAC-MD5), Replay Detection Method (RDM) 0, and a Replay Detection value set according to the RDM.

The Authentication Information begins with a Type byte followed by a 128-bit Value. Type 1 means the Forcerenew nonce value, used in the ACK message. Type 2 means the HMAC-MD5 digest of the Forcerenew message.
sections.plainLanguage: The note has labelled boxes. One box says what kind of secret stuff is inside, and another holds the secret word or the stamp.

sections.title: Server and Client Behavior
sections.content:
If a capable server gets a DISCOVER or REQUEST from a capable client and has no nonce recorded yet, it MUST generate one and put it in the ACK. The server picks a nonce only during the Request/ACK exchange, records it and sends it in an Authentication option. It SHOULD NOT repeat the nonce in an ACK to a renew unless a new one was generated. If the client moves to the REBINDING state and a new server answers, that server MUST generate a new nonce.

The nonce is 128 bits long and MUST be a cryptographically strong random or pseudo-random number that cannot easily be predicted. To authenticate a Forcerenew message, the server picks a replay detection value according to its RDM and computes an HMAC-MD5 over the entire message, following Section 21.5 of RFC 3315, with the HMAC field set to zero during the calculation.

The client MUST check that the ACK contains a Forcerenew Nonce in an authentication option. If the server advertised capability in its OFFER but the ACK omits a valid option, the client MUST discard the message and return to the INIT state. The client MUST record the nonce from any valid ACK that has one. On a Forcerenew message it computes the same HMAC-MD5 with the stored nonce and accepts the message only if the result matches.
sections.plainLanguage: The server makes up a hard-to-guess secret word and tells it to you. Later you check that the stamp on a message matches what that word would make. If it does not match, you ignore the message.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
FORCERENEW can be used in some networks to snoop and spoof traffic, so every FORCERENEW message MUST be authenticated, either with RFC 3118 or with this mechanism. As in DHCPv6, the nonce stops an off-link attacker, who does not have it, from forcing a renewal.

An on-link attacker can simply watch the renewal go out and answer it, so the mechanism does not help against on-link attacks. The RFC concludes HMAC-MD5 is adequate for the purpose and no extensible HMAC mechanism is needed. Messages that fail authentication should be silently discarded by the client.

Known weaknesses: a flood of bogus FORCERENEW messages can overwhelm the client device with authentication work, and the protocol can be compromised by an attacker who can intercept the initial message in which the server sends the nonce.
sections.plainLanguage: The secret word keeps strangers far away from tricking you. It cannot help against someone standing right next to you who hears the word, and a crowd shouting fake notes can still tire you out.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: IANA assigned a new DHCPv4 option code from the registry 'BOOTP Vendor Extensions and DHCP Options': tag 145, name FORCERENEW_NONCE_CAPABLE, data length 1, description 'Forcerenew Nonce Capable', with this document as the reference.
sections.plainLanguage: The group that keeps the official list of option numbers wrote down number 145 for this feature.
